claim: Paper is an arXiv preprint submitted 8 Oct 2026 by Lei, Lin, Lu, Torr and Zou.
quote: Submitted on 8 Oct 2026

claim: Explicit no-think controls do not reliably remove visible reasoning; the authors name this 'Thinking Inertia'.
quote: We find that explicit no-think controls cannot reliably eliminate visible inference. Models instead exhibit "Thinking Inertia": explicit inference persists even under strict controls and becomes more prevalent as the answer space opens.

claim: Six prompting interventions were tested on six LLMs across Boolean, multiple-choice and open-ended questions.
quote: We evaluate six prompting interventions on six LLMs across Boolean, multiple-choice, and open-ended questions.

claim: DeepSeek-V4-Flash shows visible explicit inference in 99.9% of open-ended responses with thinking disabled.
quote: even a frontier LLM such as DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) retains visible explicit inference in 99.9% of open-ended responses under its disabled-thinking setting.

claim: Strict answer-only prompting raises answer-only rate from near zero to ~40% but cuts accuracy ~15 points on open-ended tasks.
quote: strict answer-only prompting raises mean ETR from near zero to roughly 40% while reducing mean accuracy by about 15 percentage points.

claim: On open-ended tasks, Think-Off to Strict lowers explicit inference rate from 99.69% to 62.00%.
quote: the corresponding EIR likewise decreases from 99.69% to 62.00%

claim: Under Think-Off most models are 80-100% answer-only on yes/no tasks, but near zero on open-ended tasks.
quote: Under M2 ( Think-off ), most models reach roughly 80–100% ETR on Bool, with sharply reduced QRel. and EIR.

claim: Models tested: Qwen3-4B/32B/235B-A22B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GPT-5.4, Gemini-3-Flash; benchmarks BoolQ, StrategyQA, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, MATH.
quote: We use BoolQ [ 6 ] and StrategyQA [ 10 ] .

claim: Rewriting the same questions from multiple choice to yes/no raised answer-only rate from 10.5% to 62.5% with similar accuracy (Qwen3-32B).
quote: The Boolean rewrite leaves accuracy nearly unchanged, from 77.8% to 78.9%, but raises ETR from 10.5% to 62.5%

claim: Prefix forcing does not reliably produce answer-only responses.
quote: Prefix forcing does not reliably produce answer-only responses.

claim: GPT-5.4 is the main exception, maintaining high answer-only compliance on yes/no and multiple choice.
quote: GPT-5.4 is the main exception to this recovery pattern, maintaining high answer-only compliance and correspondingly low EIR on both Bool and MCQ.

claim: Human labels agreed 98.8% with the GPT-5.5 judge and 96.7% with a Claude Opus 4.8 judge on 600 outputs.
quote: the human explicit-inference labels achieve 98.8% mean binary agreement with the primary GPT-5.5 judge and 96.7% with the independent Claude Opus 4.8 judge across all 600 outputs.

claim: The full corpus contains 572,688 outputs.
quote: our full-corpus audit flags only 301 of 572,688 outputs (0.053%) as near-verbatim repetitions

claim: The study measures visible output only, not hidden computation.
quote: Our claims therefore concern visible output, not the absence of task-relevant computation from hidden states

claim: Authors caution that visible compliance does not imply lower inference cost.
quote: Visible compliance should not, however, be equated with lower inference cost when hidden reasoning may remain active.

claim: Authors list multilingual, code, tool-use, multi-turn and stochastic settings as untested.
quote: Generalization to multilingual, code, tool-use, multi-turn, and stochastic settings, as well as robustness to evolving proprietary endpoints, remains open.

claim: Proposed future work: train models for calibrated stopping and examine whether computation moves to a hidden channel.
quote: One direction is to train models for calibrated stopping rather than uniform suppression

claim: Authors suggest task-aware routing.
quote: This suggests task-aware routing: answer directly when the interface provides sufficient support, and preserve explicit computation when suppression would sacrifice accuracy.

claim: Author affiliations: Tsinghua, Oxford, Stanford; Kevin Qinghong Lin is project lead.
quote: <sup>1</sup> Tsinghua University · <sup>2</sup> University of Oxford · <sup>3</sup> Stanford University

claim: Authors claim NeurIPS 2026 poster acceptance (UNVERIFIED: not found in NeurIPS 2026 orals/posters data as of 2026-10-14).
quote: 2026.09 — Our paper is accepted as a Poster at NeurIPS 2026!

claim: First author describes it as NeurIPS 2026 work on HF Daily Papers.
quote: Knowing when NOT to think may be just as important as knowing how to think.

claim: Paper has 215 upvotes on HF Daily Papers, listed 13 Oct 2026.
quote: "upvotes":215

claim: HF commenter questions the premise: models trained to think will think.
quote: I don't understand what this paper is getting at. Like, yeah, if you train a model to think, it'll think.

claim: Social discussion is thin; digg aggregation of X posts shows little discussion.
quote: Not enough discussion yet

claim: Prior work already found reasoning models don't always follow skip-thinking instructions.
quote: Zhu et al. (2025a) find that LRMs do not always follow the instruction to skip thinking under NoThinking setting.

claim: Counter-evidence: bypassing thinking via prompting can be effective at matched token budgets.
quote: bypassing the thinking process via simple prompting, denoted as NoThinking, can be surprisingly effective.

claim: Visible chain-of-thought is not always faithful to the model's actual reasoning.
quote: the effectiveness of such monitoring hinges on CoTs faithfully representing models' actual reasoning processes.

claim: Related: Thinkless trains models to choose when to think, cutting long-chain thinking 50-90%.
quote: Thinkless is able to reduce the usage of long-chain thinking by 50% - 90%
